title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is the use of copyrighted recordings to train a commercial AI music generation system without the rights holders' authorization. This happened at the data-collection and model-training stage, before any product reached users. Catching it would have required a rights-clearance review of the training corpus before training began, a step that was not established as having occurred.

The legal picture is layered. Universal Music Group settled and moved toward a licensing arrangement. Warner Music Group reached a similar resolution. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit alleging roughly 30,000 recordings were used without permission, and a court declined to let Sony add those recordings to its original case, leading Sony to file a new action. A class action brought by independent artists was allowed to proceed, though it was moved to a different jurisdiction. None of these lawsuits has produced a final verdict on infringement, and allegations in complaints are not established findings of fact.

What is established is that training an AI system on commercially released recordings created legal exposure that post-hoc licensing agreements can partially address but cannot retroactively eliminate. The settlements and licensing deals that followed show one path the industry is negotiating, but the ongoing Sony litigation and the independent artists' class action indicate that path remains contested.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled its lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to resolve disputes over copyright infringement. The music company had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs, including The Temptations' "My Girl," to train its artificial intelligence system without permission. Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs through text prompts.

This marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label. The company, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including will.i.am, will compensate artists who opt into the new platform, though specific financial terms were not disclosed. UMG's leadership stated the deal reflects their commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technologies and developing new business models in the evolving AI music landscape.
